list.listitem: Use provocative maneuvers to elicit symptoms of thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS). C
Urgent evaluation of vascular abnormalities should be performed with Doppler ultrasound. C
MRI gives adequate information for all types of TOS and can help rule out other diagnoses. C
Mild or intermittent symptoms of TOS should be treated with at least 6 weeks to 8 weeks of physical therapy and activity modification. C
Patients with significant arterial compromise or venous blockage with thrombus should undergo surgical decompression to prevent complications. B
Surgery can be considered selectively for other patients with persistent symptoms despite conservative therapy, but only after careful counseling regarding expected benefits. B

background.definition: TOS refers to a variety of symptoms resulting from compression of the brachial plexus and subclavian vascular structures. Symptom severity ranges from mild intermittent posture-dependent symptoms to significant compression with permanent vascular and nerve lesions. There is a lack of generally accepted criteria for diagnosing TOS.

list.listitem: All three types of TOS occur in children. vTOS in children is often due to the presence of hypercoagulable states and sports-related injuries. Boney abnormalities appear to be more frequently associated in nTOS and aTOS in children compared to adults.
The incidence is controversial because population prevalence has varied from 0.0005% to 8% in some studies.
The reported prevalence varies with geographical location.
Women are three to four times more likely to develop neurogenic TOS.
vTOS is more common in competitive athletic men versus women but incidence is equal between non-athletic men and women.

Positional or permanent compression of the brachial plexus and/or subclavian vessels is due to one or several of the following causes: Trauma resulting in remodeling or scar tissue formation. Congenital causes such as a cervical rib or narrow scalene insertion sites. Macromastia. Repetitive motions leading to muscle hypertrophy
A meta-analysis of 141 studies with 77,924 participants found that cervical ribs are present in 29% of persons with thoracic outlet syndrome and 1% of those without.

Vessels and nerves from the thorax and cervical region to the axilla pass through 3 channels: between the anterior and middle scalene muscles, through the costoclavicular space, and under the pectoralis minor tendon.
Anatomic or functional characteristics that narrow any of these channels may cause compression of the vessels and nerves, resulting in symptoms of TOS.

A study of cadavers identified histological changes, including epineurial and perineurial fibrosis, vascular hyalinization, mucinous degeneration, and frequent intraneural collagenous nodules, due to the compression from cervical ribs in the lower trunk of the brachial plexus that were not present in specimens without cervical ribs.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Postural factors such as backpack use and forward sitting position
Sagging musculature from age or obesity

list.listitem: Physical examination should consist of a minimum of 2 provocative maneuvers to elicit symptoms of TOS. Patients with 2 or more positive tests warrant further investigation. C
Patients with significant vascular compromise on examination should be investigated urgently with Doppler ultrasound to avoid the complications of ischemia and thrombotic events. B
If cervical radiographs are unhelpful, an MRI will give adequate information for all types of TOS and will help rule out other diagnoses. C
Electrophysiology studies are usually negative in TOS but are effective in ruling out other neurologic diagnoses. C
Approximately 95% of patients with TOS have symptoms related to brachial plexus compression, such as numbness, pain, or paresthesias, usually in the ulnar nerve distribution.
TOS can occasionally occur in the chest, neck, and occiput. Reports indicate a 3:1 female to male ratio of this type of TOS.
Some atrophy of the abductor pollicis brevis, interossei, and hypothenar muscles may also be present.
1.5% to 4% of cases is due to venous compression and result in upper extremity swelling, fatigue, venous distention, and cyanosis. Men are reported to have this variety slightly more than women.

Arterial obstruction comprises about 1% of cases, with symptoms of upper extremity pallor, claudication, fatigue, coolness, and possibly ulcerations. The incidence of this type is equal in men and women.
Symptoms are usually increased with repeated upper-extremity use, overhead activities, carrying motions, or any motion that stretches the brachial plexus.
See for a description of how to perform specific provocative maneuvers for TOS and the history and physical examination table for information on how to interpret them individually and in combination.

In one prospective study, false-positive tests were found in 9% to 47% of the provocative tests performed in healthy subjects with 56% of these subjects having at least 1 abnormal test. For patients with carpel tunnel syndrome, the range of false-positive tests was 42% to 77% with at least 1 abnormal test in 94% of patients.

Authors of another paper note that sonographic evaluation of asymptomatic healthy individuals may also show positive test responses from extreme arm positions; in this study, 8 of 31 had false-positive tests (complete lack of blood flow with arm positioning).
Consider latent TOS due to neurovascular compression in patients with pectus excavatum who undergo Nuss procedure
Differential diagnoses to consider include: pectoralis minor syndrome (PMS), pathologies involving the brachial pexus, cervical spine, shoulder, and elbow.
Cervical spine and CXRs are recommended to rule out cervical stenosis, cervical ribs, rib/clavicular fracture calluses and long transverse cervical processes as possible causes for symptoms.
Over 90% of aTOS cases have boney abnormalities that can be visualzied on radiographs.
Doppler ultrasound is a good initial test for evaluation of the patient with suspected vascular involvement. Combination use with 2 or more abnormal provocative maneuvers improves specificity.

Helical CT with angiography has relatively low sensitivity for venous and arterial lesions and does not give accurate information for the brachial plexus. This study may be helpful for selecting the best surgical approach and technique for vascular TOS.

Anterior scalene muscle block using electrophysiologic guidance to prevent inadvertent somatic or sympathetic ganglion blockade is very sensitive and specific for neurogenic TOS. In addition, patients with improved symptoms after scalene block tended to have good outcomes after surgery (94%).
Consider using the Society of Vascular Surgery response to scalene injection criteria to define nTOS.

Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance angiography offers excellent visualization of vessels and is useful for the detection of vTOS. MR neurogram aids in the diagnosis of nTOS by detecting compression of the brachial plexus. MRA has a highly variable sensitivity ranging from 30% to 100% over several studies, but specificity was 100% for all studies. An evidence-based review questioned the validity of these studies, however, and recommended that clinicians always carefully correlate clinical signs and symptoms of arterial occlusion with MRA findings.

Electrodiagnostic testing with median, ulnar, and medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve conductions plus needle examination demonstrated a sensitivity of 70% and a specificity of 100%. This is the recommended test to evaluate neurogenic TOS, as it helps to rule out other diagnoses, but a negative test does not rule out TOS.
Angiography has been considered the gold standard for evaluating compression of the arterial structures, but it is quite invasive. It is also ineffective in evaluation of the brachial plexus.
There is a lack of generally accepted diagnostic criteria for TOS.
See for a suggested approach to management of the patient with TOS.

The symptoms of TOS can critically impact daily living. The Functional Evaluation in Thoracic Outlet Syndrome (FETOS) is a self-questionnaire to assess the impact of TOS on patients. FETOS has moderate validity, sensitivity to change and good reproducibility.
Mild or intermittent symptoms of TOS should initially be treated with physical therapy and activity modification. C

Anterior scalene muscle blocks aid in diagnosis, may provide temporary relief of symptoms, and help determine those patients who will respond favorably to surgery. B Electrophysiologic and ultasounography guidance aids in accurate placement of the block. B
Patients who have significant arterial compromise or venous blockage with thrombus should undergo surgical decompression to prevent complications. B

Patients with muscle atrophy not due to other neurologic cause, who have significant improvement of symptoms with anterior scalene block, or who have failed conservative measures and desire further treatment, may benefit from surgical correction of the thoracic outlet after counseling. B
Incidentally found CR ribs in asymptomatic patients should be counseled to seek appropriate workup and treatment if symptoms should develop.
Consider analgesics (NSAIDs and/or opioids) for neuropathic pain, as well as muscle relaxants, anticonvulsants, and/or antidepressants as adjuvants.
Interscalene injections of steroids or botulinum toxin type A have been succesful in observational studies but a RCT failed to demonstrate significant benefit.
In general, there is a lack of high quality evidence assessing treatments in TOS.

Transaxillary first rib resection (TFRR) is the most widely used first procedure followed by supraclavicular neuroplasty of the brachial plexus (SNBP). Some surgeons use TFRR first for vascular TOS and SNBP for neurogenic TOS.
Very low quality evidence indicates that TFRR decreased pain more than SNBP, but there is no RCT evidence that either procedure is better than placebo.
An RCT comparing the 2 procedures resulted in a good or excellent outcome in 75% of the TFRR group compared with 48% in the SNBP group.
Success reports for surgery range from 43% to 90%; follow patients for at least 18 months after surgery to ensure that symptoms do not recur because of scarring. B

A 10 year review of patients who underwent first rib resection for all TOS variants showed positive outcomes in 93% in the first 5 years and 96% in the second 5-years. Complications included pneumothoraces (23%), wound infections (1.3%) and to a lesser extent hemtomas, hemothoraces and venous injury.

Thoracic outlet decompression for venous TOS combined with intraoperative percutaneous angioplasty was effective for treating residual subclavian vein stenosis, which then reduced the risk of postoperative or recurrent thrombosis. B

Stent-graft reconstruction of subclavian artery aneurysms have proven to be successful in aTOS. Although surgical complications are rare life-long surveillance is required to monitor for late graft thrombosis or stenosis.
Early surgical decompression of the brachial plexus in carefully selected pediatric patients with nTOS resulted in excellent pain relief.

A small study in 38 patients with nonspecific TOS compared ropivacaine injections in the belly of the anterior and middle scalene muscles with a sham intervention. At 4 weeks there was some improvement in function which persisted at 12 weeks.

For patients requiring thoracic outlet decompression following thrombolysis for upper extremity DVT, a systematic review identified 6 studies with 126 patients. They concluded based on limited evidence that early decompression within two weeks was comparable to later decompression in terms of safety and efficacy.
Conservative therapies consisting of posture correction, avoiding aggravating activity, and use of exercises to strengthen the thoracic outlet are mostly based on opinion.
Patients with intermittent or mild symptoms without muscle atrophy or evidence of thrombus or vascular compromise may benefit from a 6-week to 8-week trial of conservative therapy first.
One study evaluating the effectiveness of therapy to restore cervical spine motion and upper thoracic aperture reported 88% satisfaction in symptom improvement and 80% improvement in range of motion.

Another study evaluated physiotherapy techniques involving graduated resisted shoulder elevation exercises and reported 100% relief of symptoms for the patients involved. Although these are excellent results, the number of participants was limited to 8.

Incorporating traditional Korean medicine (TKM) and traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), specifically accpuncture can be considered for the non-surgical treatment of TOS. More evidence of the safety and effectiveness of traditional medicie is needed as there are limited studies assessing th benefit outside of clinical practice.
One study found satisfactory relief of TOS for up to 2 years after physical therapy. B
One study found good short and long-term results following CR resection for TOS with 64% of patients returning to normal work acitvities compared to 27% prior to the procedure.
Success reports for surgical treatment vary from 43% to 90%. B
Clinical tests for TOS in one study were not reliable indicators of prognosis.
Long-term outcomes are better predicted by factors including age, tobacco use, comorbidities, and chronic narcotic use than response to anterior scalene blocks.

algorithm.title: Evaluation and Treatment of the Patient with Suspected Thoracic Outlet Syndrome.

cell.label: Physical examination shows severe neurologic signs, muscle wasting, or venous or arterial blockage?
Refer for specialty evaluation and management.
Two or more provocative maneuvers positive (see ).
Evaluate further with chest and cervical x-rays to rule out cervical rib or bony lesion. Abnormality relating to symptoms seen on plain film?
Symptoms mild, position dependent, and tolerable?

Consult with specialty service for further management. Consider alternative diagnoses. Consider addition of the following: (1) Advanced imaging with MRI of the cervicothoracic spine from C4 to T5. (2) Electrodiagnostic studies to assist with ruling out alternative diagnoses. (3) Upper extremity Doppler study for evaluation of vascular symptoms. (4) Anterior scalene block to evaluate symptom relief and potential for surgical correction.
Refer for conservative treatment with 6-8 wk of physical therapy. Relief of symptoms?

footnotes.footnote: Signs and symptoms Neurological: numbness, pain, and paresthesias usually in ulnar nerve distribution. Possible atrophy of the abductor pollicis brevis, interossei, and hypothenar muscles. Venous: upper extremity swelling, fatigue, venous distention, and cyanosis. Arterial: upper extremity pallor, claudication, fatigue, coolness, and possible ulcerations. Symptoms increase with repeated upper extremity use, overhead activities, carrying motions, and motions that stretch the brachial plexus.

feature.caption: How to Perform Specific Provocative Tests for TOS.

tr.td: The patient inhales deeply and holds the breath while fully extending the neck and rotating the head toward the side being examined. A positive test is abolition of the radial pulse and/or replication of symptoms.
The arms are abducted and elevated with elbows bent. The patient inhales deeply; a positive test is pulse abolition.
The arms are abducted and elevated with elbows bent. The patient inhales deeply; a positive test is symptom reproduction.

The arms start in a neutral position at the patient's sides. Arms are then abducted to 30°, 60°, 90°, and 180° while the radial pulse is palpated. The angle at which the radial pulse is abolished is noted.
The arms start in a neutral position at the patient's sides. Arms are then abducted to 30°, 60°, 90°, and 180° while the radial pulse is palpated. The angle at which symptoms are reproduced is noted.

For a minimum of 3 min, the patient repeatedly clenches and unclenches the fists while keeping the arms abducted to 90° and externally rotated with palms facing upward and forward. The elbows are also braced slightly back of the frontal plane. A positive test reproduces the patient's symptoms.
Finger pressure and percussion of the supraclavicular and infraclavicular areas. A positive test replicates the patient's symptoms.
